We note that $n=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $n$ and ${n}^{2}.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(n,{n}^{2})={n}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${n}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}} & =\frac{6}{n} \\ {n}^{2}(\frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+\frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}}) & ={n}^{2}(\frac{6}{n}) \\ {n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+{n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}} & ={n}^{2}\cdot \frac{6}{n} \\ {n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n+7}{{n}^{2}}+{n}^{2}\cdot \frac{n-5}{{n}^{2}} & =n\cdot n\cdot \frac{6}{n} \\ \cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot \frac{n+7}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}}+\cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot \frac{n-5}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}} & =n\cdot \cancel{n}\cdot \frac{6}{\cancel{n}} \\ n+7+n-5 & =n\cdot 6\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $n,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}n+7+n-5 & =n\cdot 6 \\ 2n+2 & =6n \\ -4n & =-2 \\ n & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $n=0$ as a solution. But since $n=\frac{1}{2}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $n=\frac{1}{2}.$
